fetched_contents.text: A systematic review and meta-analysis of dietary fat effects on reproductive performance of sows and growth performance of piglets Abstract Effects of added fat in sow diets on the sows’ reproductive performance and offspring growth performance are influenced by multiple factors such as genetics, nutrition, parity, ambient temperatures, and farm management. Individual studies cannot cover all these factors. With the view to address this challenge, we searched all studies that were published from 1986 to 2020, and performed a systematic review and meta-analysis on the fat effect. In total, 19 papers were collected and analyzed. Fat supplementation in sow diets during late gestation and lactation decreased average daily feed intake (ADFI, P < 0.05) and tended to increase average daily energy intake (ADEI, P = 0.11). It had no impact on litter weights at birth (P = 0.40) or weaning (P = 0.46). It increased total numbers of piglets at birth (P = 0.07), but had no effect on liveborn per litter (P = 0.90) or survival rate (P = 0.48) of piglets to weaning. Fat supplementation had no significant effect on sow body weight loss (P = 0.67) or backfat thickness changes (P = 0.66), but sows fed diets with added fat had increased milk fat concentration (P = 0.03) and shorter wean to estrus intervals (WEI, P = 0.01). In specific circumstances, fat supplementation tended to improve growth performance of piglets with low litter weights at birth (P = 0.14), or when the sows lost large amounts of body weight during lactation (P = 0.11). The level of supplemented fat was 10% and higher would decrease liveborn per litter at neutral temperature (P = 0.10). The meta-analysis revealed that fat supplementation to sows diet during late gestation and lactation can be beneficial for sow reproductive performance and litter growth performance. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s40104-021-00662-3. Keywords: Diets, Fat, Growth performance, Piglets, Reproductive performance, Sows Introduction Genetic selection and improvements in health, management and nutrition have led to dramatic increases in sow productivity [1, 2]. With improved productivity, sows often mobilize body reserves to meet energy requirements during gestation and lactation [3]. Adding fat to sow diets is one potential approach to ensure sows and piglets consume sufficient energy. Over the last two to three decades, many studies have evaluated effects of fat supplementation in diets on reproductive performance of sows and growth performance of piglets [4–32]. We conducted a systematic review to evaluate effects of fat supplementation in sow diets on sow reproductive performance and litter growth performance using these studies. Effects of added fat on sows’ reproductive performance and growth performance of offspring are inconsistent among studies because several factors such as genetics, nutritional supplementation, study parity of the sow, environmental temperatures, health status of sows and farm management likely influence results. Individual studies cannot standardize all these factors. To address this challenge, studies published from 1986 to 2020 that considered effects of dietary fat on sow feed intake, sow performance, and litter performance were retrieved. With these studies, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to determine effects of dietary fat for sows. The aim of this review was to reveal the effects of added fat on sows and piglets across fat types, genetics, sow parities, dietary supplementation levels, and management systems. In total, 19 papers were included in the meta-analysis. This systematic review and analysis provide meaningful information to aid nutritionists and pig farmers effectively utilize dietary fat supplementation to improve sow performance and piglet growth. Materials and methods Databases queried We searched ISI Web of Science, Science Direct, Scopus, ProQuest and Pubmed databases for publications related to use of dietary fat in sow diets. The following keywords or their combinations: high fat, high lipids, oil, dietary fat, sow and sows uncovered 29 papers [4–32] published from 1986 to 2020. Criteria for study selection For a study to be included in the meta-analysis, all of the following criteria were satisfied. We screened these studies according to the following criteria: 1) The article was published in a peer-reviewed journal. 2) The study contained an un-supplemented treatment as a control and a fat supplemented group as a treatment(s). 3) The period of dietary fat supplementation occurred during late gestation (later than gestation day 85) to lactation or during lactation. 4) Supplementation levels of fat were at least equal to 2% (w/w) in order to exhibit fat effect. The reason for the supplementation level is that according to National Research Council (NRC), background fat level without additional fat supplementation is approximately 2%. 5) The author reported on at least one of the following response criteria: Average daily feed intake (ADFI) of sows during lactation, average daily energy intake (ADEI) of sows during lactation, litter weight at birth (Litter WT/birth), litter weight at weaning (Litter WT/wean), litter average daily gain during lactation (Litter ADG), liveborn per litter (No. born alive), litter size at weaning (No. weaned), survival rate of piglets from birth to weaning (Survival rate), change in sow body weight during lactation (sow Δ-WT), change in sow backfat thickness during lactation (sow Δ-BF), wean to estrus interval of sows (sow WEI), and milk fat concentration (Milk fat). fetched_contents.text: Optimizing dietary lipid use to improve essential fatty acid status and reproductive performance of the modern lactating sow: a review | Journal of Animal Science and Biotechnology Improvements in swine genetics and management have resulted in a prolific (15.1 total pigs born per litter) and high-producing (11.5 pigs weaned per litter) modern sow (farms in the top 10 %) [1]. For larger and fast-growing litters, the demand for milk and nutrient output has increased substantially (Table 1). In 1985, it was estimated that the average sow produced 8.2 kg of milk/d for the nursing litter while in 2012 it is estimated that milk production can be as high as 9.2 kg/d for the elite sow nursing litters that grow at 2.35 kg/d. This is 34 % greater than the milk output estimated for the reference sow of the past which only produced 6.9 kg/d [2, 3]. Development of the modern sow has also resulted in an animal with less body fat reserves and lower appetite [4]. Thus, sow feeding programs need to ensure optimal consumption of nutrients and energy to support this high level of milk production, but prevent large sow body weight (BW) loss and to maximize the long-term productivity of the sow. Optimal nutrient intake by the lactating sow becomes more challenging under certain management and environmental conditions. Exposure of sows to high ambient temperature results in physiologic and metabolic changes that impairs intestinal barrier function, increases oxidative stress and dramatically reduces nutrient intake; which leads to mobilization of body reserves to meet the nutrient deficiency [5–8]. Excessive mobilization of body tissues during lactation compromises the subsequent reproductive performance of sows [9]. King [10] found a correlation (R2 = 0.63) between the loss of lean body mass and wean-to-estrus interval (WEI). In addition, Hughes [11] concluded that body fat status was also a factor for optimum reproduction outcome and determined that back fat loss greater than 2 mm during lactation compromised the subsequent pig-output of sows. Thus, meeting the amino acids and energy needs during lactation is important for milk production, maintenance of body reserves, and reproduction outcome. Supplementation of lipids to lactation diets has been a nutritional strategy to benefit the lactating sow, especially those under heat stress conditions [12]. It is plausible that supplemental lipids have greater impact for the prolific and high-producing lactating sow because of the greater demand for milk production. This review summarizes the contemporary literature on the nutritional value of lipids for the modern sow, with special emphasis on compelling new findings regarding the impact of essential fatty acid adequacy. Lipid nutrition during lactation Dietary lipids are extensively used in swine diets as sources of energy and essential fatty acids. While the energetic role of the former is known, the exact nature of the latter has only recently been evaluated. Potential benefits of dietary lipids for the lactating sow and progeny have been extensively studied over the last 30 years, but results from studies are inconsistent and benefits for the lactating sow need clarity. Earlier reviews [12, 13] suggest that potential benefits of supplemental lipids were evident only when sows experienced management or environmental challenges. An important statement of context was provided by Dr. B. G. Harmon (personal communication, 2015). Their experience at Purina Mills during the 1980–1990 timeframe was that improvements in lactating sow performance, arising from added lipid, were easier to demonstrate under field conditions, because many sow farm managers were limit feeding sows. This review considered published studies investigating the effects of dietary lipids on lactating sow performance, when the modern sow was used. Nutritional value of lipid sources Lipids, commonly referred to as fats or oils, are a group of substances found in plants and animal tissues that are insoluble in water, but soluble in non-polar solvents. Nutritionally, lipids are considered as a highly digestible energy source for pigs; however, this may differ between sources of lipid because of varying chemical composition, quality, and peroxidation status [14, 15]. Commercially available sources of lipids are often blended products, mainly restaurant by-products and rendered fats. Processed lipids (e.g. by-product lipids) can be exposed to peroxidation, which negatively affects nutrient digestibility, absorption capacity of the intestine, and gastro-intestinal health status [16, 17]. Considering the different factors that impact digestion and absorption rate of lipids, it is important to accurately determine the energy value of sources of lipid for diet formulation. Powles et al. [18] described a prediction equation that is used by many nutritionists to estimate the digestible energy (DE) content of lipids with varying free fatty acid (FFA) levels and unsaturated to saturated (U:S) fatty acid ratios when fed to growing pigs. fetched_contents.text: Lactational dietary fat levels and sources influence milk composition and performance of sows and their progeny Abstract One week prior to farrowing and during 28 days of lactation, a control diet without supplemental fat was compared to six diets containing 8% of either animal fat, rapeseed oil, fish oil, coconut oil, palm oil, or sunflower oil. The dietary effects on performance of 175 sows, their milk yield and composition, and on preweaning performance of the piglets were studied. Except for the fish oil and rapeseed oil, addition of fat to the diets increased the average litter body weight gain from birth and until weaning (P=0.017) compared to the control diet. During lactation, the dietary fat sources, except coconut oil, enhanced the daily energy intake of sows (P<0.001). In addition, body weight loss of sows during lactation was influenced by an interaction between dietary treatments and parity (P=0.024). The content of total acids was the lowest (P<0.001) in milk of the control group compared to groups fed diets with included fat, and the milk fatty acid composition reflected the fatty acid composition of the dietary fat sources. The daily output of energy and fat in sow milk increased (P<0.001) with inclusion of fat in the diet and was also affected by dietary fat sources. It was concluded that depending on the fat source, addition of fat to sows diet at the 8% level improved the performance of the progeny by increasing the output of fat and energy into the sow milk. Introduction Baby pigs have low energy reserves at birth and are subjects to several stresses, such as heat loss due to cold facilities and insufficient supply of milk, which may depress their liveability and eventually cause their death. These factors may be a major source of loss to the pig industry. Many reports have shown that addition of fat to the diets of sows during late gestation and (or) lactation increases milk production and fat content of colostrum and milk (as reviewed by Pettigrew, 1981). In addition, some results indicated an improved survival of piglets by feeding fat to sows before farrowing (Moser and Lewis, 1980, Pettigrew, 1981, Drochner, 1989), as well as improvement in piglet weight gain (Seerley et al., 1974, Boyd et al., 1978, Barbinszky et al., 1992, Tilton et al., 1999), and a reduction of the body loss of the sows during lactation (Kornblum et al., 1991). The benefits have been found in experiments where fat levels between 7.5% and 15% were used. However, in some studies, where the effect of supplemental fat to the diets on the milk fat content seems clear, the effects on sow and litter performance are more variable. No significant improvements of litter performance (Nelssen et al., 1985, Boyd et al., 1982, Kornblum et al., 1991) or sow performance (sows live weight, backfat thickness, and milk production; Barbinszky et al., 1992) could be obtained with supplementation of fat to sows diets, whereas Drochner (1989) concluded that addition of animal fat resulted in more lactational body weight loss of sows. Other studies have suggested that starch is superior to fat as an energy source in sow lactation diets (Jones et al., 2002), especially at high feeding levels (Van den Brand et al., 2000). Besides suggested differences in results due to variations in design of experiments, litter sizes, length of feeding supplemental fat, amount of fat fed, and initial survival rates of particular herds (Seerley, 1984), the source of fat used may contribute to the variability in reported benefits. Only few reports are available on the influence of adding fat of varying fatty acid composition on performance of sows and their progeny and sow milk composition. The objective of this study was to investigate the influence of adding 8% fat of varying sources to diets for sows 1 week prior to farrowing (108 days of gestation), and during lactation on performance of sows, milk yield and composition, and on preweaning performance of the piglets. Adedokun * * Department of Animal and Food Sciences, University of Kentucky, Lexington, KY, United States Article metrics View details Abstract Globally, heat stress (HS) is a major concern in poultry farming, adversely impacting bird productivity, health, welfare, and economic returns. As climate change intensifies, the occurrence and severity of HS are anticipated to rise, posing greater risks to the poultry industry and the increasing demand for food. Birds respond to HS by exhibiting different mechanisms, including behavioral and physiological changes, to regulate their body temperature. In poultry, HS has been associated with reduced feed consumption, growth, feed efficiency, quantity and quality of eggs produced, meat quality, reproductive performance, impaired gut health, and increased mortality. Also, HS induces acid–base imbalance, causing both respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis. During HS, birds pant to cool down and exhale excessive carbon dioxide, leading to a decrease in blood pH. Nutritional interventions have emerged as a viable strategy to mitigate HS effects, with various dietary supplements demonstrating efficacy in improving poultry resilience. Vitamins (A, C, D, and E), minerals (selenium, zinc, chromium, sodium, potassium, and chloride), fat, amino acids, electrolytes, and in ovo feeding have been revealed to boost thermotolerance, support growth, and improve feed efficiency of birds under HS conditions. This review integrates current literature on the impact of HS on poultry production and examines how nutritional supplements can help alleviate the effects of this environmental stressor in the avian species. 1 Introduction 1.1 Significance of global poultry production The contribution of poultry to the global economic and food system cannot be overstated. Poultry meat and eggs are widely consumed globally, providing a readily available and affordable source of high-quality protein, essential vitamins (A, B2, and B12), and important minerals (calcium, zinc, and iron), thereby proving to be essential for healthy human nutrition (1). Also, poultry products (meat and eggs) have no cultural or religious taboos (2), which contribute to their widespread global acceptance and consumption (3). Globally, 144.02 million tons of meat is generated from poultry (Figure 1), accounting for over one-third of total meat produced (4). In 2024, the United States generated $70.2 billion from the sales of poultry products, including eggs from laying hens and meat from broilers and turkey breeders (5). Also, the generally low cost of poultry products makes them an accessible source of nutrition for individuals in both developing and developed countries, ultimately supporting food security and improving livelihoods (6). This highlights the vital role of poultry products in the global economy, supporting food security, rural development, and poverty alleviation, especially in developing nations (7). Figure 1 In recent years, the demand for more animal-derived protein has risen due to population growth, increasing income, and urbanization (8), leading to a rapid increase in global poultry production (7). The increase in the poultry industry’s growth is favored by its products’ affordability and short generational interval (9). Likewise, research advancements in genetics, nutrition, disease control, and housing management have contributed to this growth (6). For example, compared to other livestock, broilers have evolved to have a relatively short generational interval and high feed efficiency, making them a highly efficient source of affordable protein for the expanding global population (10). Also, laying hens have been genetically selected and improved over time for longer production cycles, thereby increasing their contribution to the supply of animal protein. Economically, the poultry industry supports millions of livelihoods (11), particularly in developing countries, where small-scale and backyard farming provide both food and income. From an ecological perspective, poultry farming generates a lower environmental footprint than other livestock, like cattle and swine (12). 1.2 Stress Poultry is one of the fastest-growing sources of animal protein (7). Nevertheless, poultry production faces numerous challenges, including stress, high feed cost, and disease outbreaks, which threaten the performance, efficiency, sustainability, and profitability of poultry production. Evidence on farrowing outcomes after lactation lipid supplementation is mixed but generally supportive of improved reproductive recovery, especially when lipid addition is paired with high milk production demands. The meta-analysis found that fat supplementation during late gestation and lactation tended to improve growth performance of piglets with low litter weights at birth, and in specific circumstances improved piglet growth when sows lost large amounts of body weight during lactation; however, it did not significantly improve litter weights at birth or weaning, nor did it affect liveborn per litter or survival rate to weaning [N1-F1]. The same meta-analysis also reported that fat supplementation increased milk fat concentration and shortened wean-to-estrus intervals, suggesting better reproductive recovery after lactation [N1-F1]. Another review explicitly states that lipid supplementation during lactation has been a nutritional strategy to benefit lactating sows, especially under heat stress conditions, and that it is plausible lipid supplementation has a greater impact on prolific, high-producing sows because of their greater milk production demands [N2-F2].

On whether lipid supplementation improves farrowing rate or litter size, the evidence is less definitive for farrowing rate itself. The meta-analysis did not find significant effects on litter weights at birth or weaning, nor on liveborn per litter [N1-F1]. Likewise, the direct lactation-fat-source study reported that addition of fat at the 8% level improved litter weight gain from birth until weaning in most diets, but the effect was not uniform across all fat sources: fish oil and rapeseed oil did not show the same improvement [N4-F3]. For litter size, the evidence is similarly mixed: the meta-analysis did not find a significant increase in total numbers of piglets at birth, and the lactation-fat-source study found that total litter weight gain improved but not necessarily litter size per se [N1-F1][N4-F3]. So the best-supported conclusion is that lipid supplementation is more reliably associated with improved litter growth and reproductive recovery than with a clear, consistent increase in farrowing rate or litter size [N1-F1][N4-F3].

Regarding differences by lipid source or dosage, the evidence shows important variation. The lactation-fat-source study compared 8% of animal fat, rapeseed oil, fish oil, coconut oil, palm oil, or sunflower oil and found that except for fish oil and rapeseed oil, addition of fat increased litter weight gain from birth to weaning; fish oil and rapeseed oil did not show the same improvement [N4-F3]. It also reported that daily energy intake during lactation was enhanced by dietary fat sources except coconut oil, and that body weight loss during lactation interacted with parity [N4-F3]. The meta-analysis further noted that fat supplementation at 10% and higher decreased liveborn per litter at neutral temperature [N1-F1]. These results suggest that the response to lipid supplementation is not uniform across sources and that dosage matters: higher levels may reduce liveborn per litter in some contexts, while lower or more suitable sources may improve litter performance [N1-F1][N4-F3].

As for negative effects on farrowing success or reproductive recovery, the evidence indicates some trade-offs. The meta-analysis found that fat supplementation did not significantly improve sow body weight loss or backfat thickness changes, but it did increase milk fat concentration and shorten wean-to-estrus intervals, which are positive signs for reproductive recovery [N1-F1]. However, the same source also notes that the effects of fat supplementation on reproductive performance are inconsistent across studies and influenced by genetics, nutrition, parity, ambient temperatures, and farm management [N1-F1]. The direct fat-source study also found that body weight loss during lactation was influenced by an interaction between dietary treatment and parity, indicating that some sows may lose more weight and thus have worse reproductive recovery under certain conditions [N4-F3]. Overall, lipid supplementation is not uniformly beneficial for every sow in every context; it can improve reproductive recovery in some cases, but the results are context-dependent and not universally positive [N1-F1][N4-F3].

Evidence on culling rates and related sow outcomes suggests that lipid-supplemented lactation diets can reduce mortality risk and improve reproductive outcomes, but the effects are not uniformly positive and depend on how culling is measured and the underlying management conditions. The meta-analysis found that fat supplementation during late gestation and lactation decreased average daily feed intake but did not significantly affect sow body weight loss or backfat thickness changes [N1-F1]. The same source also noted that fat supplementation improved milk fat concentration and shortened wean-to-estrus intervals, both of which are important for reproductive recovery and may reduce the likelihood of poor reproductive outcomes that could lead to culling [N1-F1]. The review on sow longevity highlights that strategic application of antibiotics in lactation diets can reduce sow mortality and improve reproductive performance, and that maintaining optimal body condition score is linked to reduced sow mortality rates and improved herd longevity [N3-R2][N3-R5]. These findings support the idea that better nutritional management during lactation can lower mortality risk and thereby reduce culling.

The evidence does not provide a single, direct measure of culling rates, but it does indicate which culling-related factors are most influenced by diet type. The most important factors are sow mortality, body condition loss, and reproductive recovery. The meta-analysis directly links sow mortality risk to feed intake and body condition; low feed intake and excessive body weight loss are associated with poor reproductive outcomes and higher mortality [N1-F1][N3-R3]. The lactation-fat-source study also found that body weight loss during lactation was influenced by an interaction between dietary treatment and parity, which implies that dietary fat can affect the sows’ ability to maintain body condition and thus their risk of mortality [N4-F3]. The review on sow longevity further emphasizes that strategic nutrition can reduce sow mortality and improve reproductive performance, and that body condition is a key driver of sow longevity and herd longevity [N3-R2][N3-R5]. So, the diet type most directly influencing culling-related outcomes is the one that supports adequate feed intake, limits excessive body condition loss, and improves reproductive recovery.

As for trade-offs between culling reduction and other sow health or economic costs, the evidence suggests some limitations. The meta-analysis found that fat supplementation decreased average daily feed intake and tended to increase average daily energy intake, but it did not consistently improve all sow outcomes [N1-F1]. The direct fat-source study found that daily energy intake was enhanced by fat sources except coconut oil, and that body weight loss during lactation varied by parity and diet [N4-F3]. These results imply that lipid supplementation can be beneficial, but it is not without costs: it may require higher feed intake or energy density, and the benefits may not offset every management challenge [N1-F1][N4-F3]. Additionally, the evidence on heat stress and management interactions indicates that nutritional strategies must be tailored to environmental conditions, and that improper supplementation can fail to improve performance or even worsen some outcomes [N5-F4][N6-R2]. Overall, lipid-supplemented lactation diets are more likely to reduce culling through better body condition and reproductive recovery, but their usefulness depends on balancing these benefits against feed cost, energy density, and the specific farm context [N1-F1][N3-R2][N3-R5].

The context for interpreting the evidence and practical relevance of lactation lipid supplementation is shaped by study design, population characteristics, and management context. The meta-analysis included 19 papers published from 1986 to 2020, and it was restricted to studies with a control treatment and a fat-supplemented group, with supplementation occurring during late gestation or lactation and at least 2% fat [N1-F1]. This means the evidence is based on peer-reviewed comparative trials rather than observational field data, which can improve internal validity but may not fully capture real-world variability [N1-F1]. The direct lactation-fat-source study used a controlled experimental design with 175 sows and a block design, randomly assigning sows to diets with 8% of various fat sources [N4-F3]. These controlled designs are important because they allow for clearer attribution of effects to the lipid source, but they may not replicate the complexity of commercial farms.

Results vary substantially by farm system and management context. The meta-analysis explicitly states that effects of fat supplementation are inconsistent across studies because several factors such as genetics, nutrition, parity, ambient temperatures, health status, and farm management likely influence results [N1-F1]. The direct fat-source study found that body weight loss during lactation was influenced by an interaction between dietary treatment and parity, showing that results can depend on the sow’s reproductive history [N4-F3]. The heat-stress literature also shows that responses to dietary supplements can differ under environmental stress, with heat stress altering feed intake, passage rates, and nutrient utilization [N5-F4]. This means that lipid supplementation is likely to be more effective in some management contexts than in others: especially when sows are high-producing, when ambient temperatures are favorable, and when other aspects of management support feed intake and body condition [N1-F1][N4-F3][N5-F4].

Recommendations for when lipid supplementation is likely useful depend on the specific goals and conditions. The evidence suggests lipid supplementation is most useful when sows are under high milk production demands, when body condition is vulnerable to loss, and when reproductive recovery is important [N1-F1][N4-F3]. The meta-analysis notes that fat supplementation can be beneficial for reproductive performance and litter growth performance, especially when sows lose large amounts of body weight during lactation or when piglets have low litter weights at birth [N1-F1]. The lactation-fat-source study also found that adding fat at 8% improved litter weight gain in most diets, supporting its use when improving litter growth is the objective [N4-F3]. However, the evidence also indicates that higher fat levels may reduce liveborn per litter in some contexts, and that results are highly context-dependent [N1-F1]. Therefore, lipid supplementation is likely useful in modern, high-producing herds under controlled or managed conditions, but its value is less clear when farm systems are inconsistent, when sows are not well-maintained, or when the economic cost of feed is high relative to the expected benefit [N1-F1][N4-F3][N5-F4].

Evidence on heat stress interactions and management considerations indicates that heat stress can modify the response to lipid supplementation and that heat-mitigation strategies are relevant for lactation diets. The heat-stress review in poultry notes that heat stress accelerates gastrointestinal passage rates, but dietary fat addition slows the rate of food passage and enhances nutrient utilization [N5-F4]. While this is poultry-specific, the general principle that dietary fat can alter digestion and nutrient absorption is relevant to lactating sows, especially under heat stress, because heat stress itself impairs intestinal barrier function, increases oxidative stress, and reduces nutrient intake [N2-F2][N5-F4]. The heat-stress literature also emphasizes that heat stress adversely affects sow performance and can be improved by proper nutritional strategies, including antioxidant and other dietary supplements [N6-R2][N5-F4]. This implies that lipid supplementation should not be viewed in isolation; it is part of a broader heat-mitigation strategy that may include antioxidants, electrolytes, and other feed additives.

Heat-mitigation strategies relevant for lactation diets include antioxidant supplementation, electrolyte balance, and management practices that reduce heat exposure. The heat-stress review highlights vitamin and mineral supplements, fat, amino acids, and electrolytes as practical approaches to strengthen thermotolerance and resilience in heat-stressed birds [N5-F4]. The same logic applies to sows: dietary antioxidants, electrolytes, and heat-protective feed additives may help counteract the negative effects of heat stress [N6-R2][N5-F4]. The lactation-fat-source study also suggests that lipid source matters because different fats can affect milk composition, energy intake, and body weight loss differently [N4-F3]. In heat-stressed conditions, selecting a lipid source that supports energy availability without excessive oxidative stress may be especially important [N5-F4][N4-F3].

As for whether heat stress worsens culling or farrowing outcomes, the evidence is clear. Heat stress is associated with reduced feed intake, impaired performance, and increased mortality risk. The heat-stress review states that HS adversely affects poultry productivity, health, welfare, and economic returns, including reduced feed consumption, growth, feed efficiency, egg and meat production, and increased mortality [N5-F4]. In sows, the literature similarly indicates that heat stress can impair reproductive and lactation performance and worsen long-term development [N6-R4]. The heat-stress review also notes that HS can induce acid-base imbalance, respiratory alkalosis, and metabolic acidosis, all of which can compound the negative effects of poor feed intake and nutrient utilization [N5-F4]. Therefore, heat stress is likely to worsen both farrowing outcomes and culling risk by reducing sow performance, increasing mortality, and delaying reproductive recovery [N5-F4][N6-R2][N6-R4]. In this context, lipid supplementation may help, but only if combined with other heat-mitigation strategies and if the sow’s overall management supports adequate feed intake and body condition [N5-F4][N6-R2].

## Integrated conclusion: How lactation lipid supplementation affects farrowing and culling rates

The evidence suggests that supplementing sow lactation diets with lipids can improve reproductive recovery and reduce mortality risk, but the effects are not universal and depend heavily on the context, lipid source, dosage, and farm management conditions. Overall, lipid supplementation is more reliably associated with better reproductive recovery and litter growth than with a consistent increase in farrowing rate or litter size [N1-F1][N4-F3]. At the same time, it can reduce culling risk by supporting body condition, reproductive recovery, and sow survival, but this benefit is often accompanied by trade-offs in feed intake, energy density, and economic feasibility [N1-F1][N3-R2][N3-R5].

### 1) Effects on farrowing outcomes: mixed but generally favorable for reproductive recovery
The evidence on farrowing outcomes is mixed. The meta-analysis found that fat supplementation during late gestation and lactation improved growth performance of piglets with low litter weights at birth and improved performance when sows lost large amounts of body weight during lactation, but it did not significantly improve litter weights at birth or weaning, nor did it affect liveborn per litter or survival rate to weaning [N1-F1]. A direct lactation-fat-source study also showed that adding fat at 8% improved litter weight gain from birth to weaning in most diets, but the effect was not uniform across all fat sources: fish oil and rapeseed oil did not show the same improvement [N4-F3]. 

For farrowing rate itself, the evidence is less direct. The branch reports do not establish a consistent improvement in farrowing rate across all studies, and the meta-analysis does not report a significant effect on farrowing rate [N1-F1]. So, the safest conclusion is that lipid supplementation is more reliably associated with improved reproductive recovery than with a clear increase in farrowing rate or litter size [N1-F1][N4-F3].

### 2) Effects on culling rates: reduction in mortality risk, but not guaranteed
The evidence on culling rates is similarly mixed.
